comparison: Perfect agreement on c-Fos immunohistochemistry findings (C1, C12-C16). Both evaluations find the data well-supported with appropriate statistical analysis. Peer reviewers explicitly accepted the findings showing differential OT neuron activation between pup care and infanticide behaviors.

Strong agreement on optogenetic activation effects in pup-care animals (C2, C19-C22). Both acknowledge sex-specific effects with males showing facilitated pup care and females showing no effect. OpenEval notes potential ceiling effects in females (C113-C115), which peer reviewers also acknowledge as 'other mechanisms may regulate female pup care.'

Agreement on optogenetic activation effects in infanticide animals (C3, C23-C26). Both find evidence solid for prolonged latency to attack. Peer reviewer appears to have misstated 'reduced' when data show 'prolonged,' but overall accepts the findings. Both note effects are consistent across sexes in infanticide animals.

Strong agreement on optogenetic inhibition findings (C4, C31-C35). Both accept the asymmetric effects where inhibition promotes infanticide but does not affect established pup care. Peer reviewers confirmed 'Suppressing activity of PVN oxytocin neurons promoted infanticide' without challenge.

Strong agreement on fiber photometry findings (C7-C8, C36-C40). Peer reviewers praised the OT GRAB sensor work as 'a major achievement' and 'valuable data.' Minor methodological questions about z-scoring and motion artifact correction were raised but do not challenge core findings.

Agreement on PVN-mPFC projection manipulation in pup-care animals (C5-C6, C49-C51). Both accept the sex-specific effects paralleling somatic activation results. Peer reviewers noted 'Stimulating PVN->mPFC OT projections facilitated pup care in males' without raising concerns about the projection-specific approach.

Perfect agreement on PVN-mPFC projection activation in infanticide animals (C52-C55). Both find evidence supports prolonged latency to approach and attack in both sexes. Peer reviewers emphasized this as demonstrating the pathway's role in 'inhibiting infanticide.'

Agreement on PVN-mPFC projection inhibition findings (C56-C60). Both accept the asymmetric effects paralleling somatic inhibition. Peer reviewers confirmed 'Inhibition of PVN->mPFC OT projections promoted infanticide' and accepted the circuit-level conclusions.

Agreement on peripheral OT administration effects (C9, C61-C68). Both find evidence supports increased pup care in males and reduced infanticide in both sexes. OpenEval notes C68 (chi-square p=0.081) is marginally non-significant, making it weakly supported. Peer reviewers praised the translational relevance.

Strong agreement on integrative conclusions (C10, C104-C106, C171). Both evaluations find the overall circuit model well-supported by convergent evidence. Editor stated 'the evidence supporting the authors' conclusions is solid' and the work 'advances our understanding of the neurobiological basis of these contrasting behaviors.'

Agreement on uncertainty regarding translational claims (C11, C107, C169-C170). Both evaluations recognize these as speculative. OpenEval explicitly states 'no clinical or wildlife studies were conducted' and 'require substantial additional research.' Peer reviewers acknowledged 'potential' applications but did not rigorously assess strength of translational claims.

Agreement on anatomical tracing data (C45-C48). Both accept the quantification of PVN projections to mPFC and other regions as supporting the circuit-specific manipulations. Peer reviewers noted this provides anatomical basis for functional findings without raising concerns.

Both address validation of optogenetic manipulations (C17-C18, C29-C30). OpenEval finds appropriate controls and validation. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted validation through praise of 'converging evidence' and multi-method approach, though one noted uncertainty about whether more OT neurons were manipulated in females.

Both address sex differences in optogenetic effects (C27-C28, C43-C44). OpenEval notes these as well-documented. Peer reviewers accepted sex differences as study strength, noting females may have 'ceiling effects of the OT system' and 'other mechanisms may regulate female pup care.'

Both address OT sensor control experiments (C41-C42). OpenEval finds controls with OTmut sensors and objects strengthen specificity. Peer reviewers praised sensor work as 'major achievement,' implicitly accepting control data, though minor methodological refinements were suggested.

Partial overlap on optogenetic findings summary (C108). OpenEval groups this with C109-C112 as summary of main optogenetic findings. Peer R2 addresses C108 as part of sex-specific activation effects in pup-care animals. Both find evidence solid.

Partial overlap on optogenetic findings summary (C111). OpenEval groups this with C108-C112 as summary. Peer R3 addresses C111 as part of infanticide animal findings. Both evaluations support the claims with solid evidence.

Partial overlap on optogenetic findings summary (C109, C112). OpenEval groups these with C108-C112 as summary of main findings. Peer R4 addresses these as part of inhibition effects. Both find evidence well-supported by experimental data.

Divergent evaluation of sex-specific effects in females (C110). OpenEval finds this well-supported as part of summary claims (C108-C112). Peer R16 expresses uncertainty, noting 'other mechanisms may regulate female pup care' and questioning whether effects on other neurotransmitters are 'not fully explored.' Ceiling effect explanation noted but not fully resolved.

OpenEval evaluated literature-based contextual claims (C113-C118) explaining sex-specific effects through citations to prior work. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims, though peer reviewers acknowledged sex differences throughout.

OpenEval evaluated extensive background and rationale claims (C69-C103) as supported by appropriate literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these background claims, as peer reviewers focused on primary experimental findings.

OpenEval evaluated discussion claims (C119-C150) contextualizing findings with literature as appropriately supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these discussion points, as peer reviewers focused on primary data and main conclusions.

OpenEval evaluated discussion claims about peripheral OT mechanisms (C151-C168) as appropriately supported by literature citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these discussion points.

OpenEval evaluated the concluding claim (C172) about advancing understanding of neural circuits as reasonable and supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing this single concluding claim, though peer reviewers affirmed overall that the work 'advances our understanding.'
